candidates.claim_content: Setting: S is a noncompact Riemann surface with Hermitian metric h, and 𝒮 is a nowhere-vanishing holomorphic 1-form with L(x)=∫_o^x 𝒮 =: x̂ a globally defined holomorphic function. Put D^𝒮(r)={x: |x̂|<r}, C^𝒮(r)={x: |x̂|=r}. dV is the Riemannian area element of h and dσ_t the Riemannian line element on C^𝒮(t). ‖𝒮_x‖_h denotes the pointwise norm of 𝒮, and the paper's own computation (Lemma 2.12) shows that the gradient of the function |x̂| has norm ‖𝒮_x‖_h and that the harmonic measure satisfies dπ_o^r = (‖𝒮‖_h/(2πr))dσ_r. The paper asserts the identity ∫_{D^𝒮(r)} k dV = ∫_0^r dt ∫_{C^𝒮(t)} k dσ_t for a (nonnegative) function k. The co-area formula actually gives ∫_{D^𝒮(r)} k dV = ∫_0^r dt ∫_{C^𝒮(t)} k/|∇|x̂|| dσ_t = ∫_0^r dt ∫_{C^𝒮(t)} (k/‖𝒮‖_h) dσ_t.

candidates.suspected_defect: The lower bound δ̄_f(a) ≥ 0 requires limsup N̄_f/T ≤ 1, which follows from N_f ≤ T+O(1) only if T^𝒮_{f,ω}(r) → ∞. In the hyperbolic case R^𝒮 < ∞ this can fail: take S = D (unit disc) with Euclidean metric, 𝒮 = dz (R^𝒮=1), f(z)=z viewed as a map into P^1(C). Then T_f(r)=∫_{r_0}^r (t/(1+t^2))dt ≤ (1/2)log 2 stays bounded, while N̄_f(r,0)=log(r/r_0) → log(1/r_0), which can be made arbitrarily large by choosing r_0 small; hence δ̄_f(0) < 0. candidates.exact_quote: In this paper, besides conditions (a) and (b), one assumes that \( \mathscr{S} \) satisfies an additional condition: \( L(x) = 0 \) if and only if \( x = o \). This condition forces \( L \) to be a univalent function.
candidates.claim_content: Setting: S is a noncompact Riemann surface, 𝒮 a holomorphic 1-form on S with (a) no zeros on S and (b) ∫_γ 𝒮 = 0 for every smooth simple closed curve γ in S, so that L(x) = ∫_o^x 𝒮 is a well-defined holomorphic function on S with nowhere-vanishing differential. The additional assumption is: L(x)=0 if and only if x=o. The paper claims this assumption forces L to be univalent (injective) on S.
candidates.suspected_defect: Having a single zero plus nonvanishing derivative does not imply global injectivity. Counterexample: S = C \ {2πik : k ∈ Z, k ≠ 0}, 𝒮 = e^z dz (nowhere zero, exact so (b) holds), L(z) = e^z − 1; the only zero of L in S is z = 0, L' = e^z ≠ 0, yet L(z)=L(z+2πi) whenever both points lie in S, so L is not univalent. Hence the claimed implication, which is later used to assert that D^𝒮(r) is simply connected and C^𝒮(r) is a simple closed curve, is unjustified.

candidates.exact_quote: Since $L$ is univalent, then $D^{\mathscr{S}}(r)$ is simply connected for all $r > 0$.
candidates.claim_content: Setting: S a noncompact Riemann surface, 𝒮 a nowhere-zero holomorphic 1-form with all periods zero, L(x)=∫_o^x 𝒮 = x̂ holomorphic with L(x)=0 iff x=o, and D^𝒮(r) = {x ∈ S : |x̂| < r}. The claim is: if L is univalent then D^𝒮(r) is simply connected for every r > 0.
candidates.suspected_defect: Univalence of L gives a biholomorphism of D^𝒮(r) onto the open set L(D^𝒮(r)) ⊂ {|w|<r}, which need not be all of {|w|<r} and need not be simply connected. Counterexample: S = D \ {1/2} with 𝒮 = dz, L(z)=z (univalent, unique zero at 0, exact form). Then D^𝒮(r) = {|z|<r} \ {1/2} for 1/2 < r < 1, which is not simply connected, although S is dz-exhausted with dz-radius 1.

candidates.claim_content: Conventions in the paper: locally dV = √(−1) h dz∧dz̄ (= 2h dξ_1∧dξ_2 with z=ξ_1+√(−1)ξ_2) and Δ = (2/h)∂^2/∂z∂z̄, i.e. the Riemannian metric is 2h(dξ_1^2+dξ_2^2). 𝒮 = φ dz, L(x)=∫_o^x 𝒮, g_r(o,x)=(1/π)log(r/|x̂|), and dπ_o^r = −(1/2)(∂g_r/∂n)dσ_r with dσ_r the Riemannian line element. In the proof a coordinate is chosen with h|_{x_0}=1, the Euclidean gradient of |L| is computed, and the identification ∂|L|/∂n = |φ(x_0)| = ‖𝒮_{x_0}‖_h is made, yielding dπ_o^r = (‖𝒮‖_h/(2πr))dσ_r.
candidates.suspected_defect: The normal derivative computed is the Euclidean one, while dσ_r is the Riemannian line element of the metric 2h(dξ_1^2+dξ_2^2). The Riemannian gradient norm of |L| is |φ|/√(2h), not |φ|/√h; at a point with h = 1 it equals |φ|/√2. So the identification ‖𝒮_{x_0}‖_h = |φ(x_0)| when h = 1 is off by √2, i.e. inconsistent with the normalization used elsewhere (e.g. ‖dz‖ = 1 for the standard Euclidean metric on C, where dV = dxdy forces h = 1/2, and ‖𝒮‖ ≡ 1 for α = (√−1/2)𝒮∧𝒮̄ in Remark 1.1, both of which correspond to ‖𝒮‖_h = |φ|/√(2h)).

candidates.claim_content: Lemma 3.6 asserts: for (S,h;𝒮) a 𝒮-exhausted Hermitian Riemann surface of 𝒮-radius R^𝒮, γ locally integrable on (0,R^𝒮) with ∫_0^{R^𝒮}γ = ∞, and k merely locally integrable on S, setting E_k(r)=∫_{C^𝒮(r)} k dπ_o^r and A_k(r)=∫_{r_0}^r (dt/t)∫_{D^𝒮(t)} k dV, one has E_k(r) ≤ (‖𝒮‖_{r,sup} r^δ γ^{2+δ}(r)/(2π)) A_k^{(1+δ)^2}(r) outside a set E_δ with ∫_{E_δ}γ < ∞. The proof applies the calculus (Borel) Lemma 3.5 twice — to rA_k'(r) and to A_k(r) — where Lemma 3.5 requires the function to be nondecreasing, of class C^1, positive at some r_0, and tending to ∞ as r → R.
candidates.suspected_defect: The hypotheses are too weak: for k not nonnegative, E_k and A_k may be negative and the fractional power A_k^{(1+δ)^2} is undefined, and the step E_k ≤ (‖𝒮‖_{r,sup}/(2πr))∫ k dσ_r uses k ≥ 0. Moreover Lemma 3.5 is invoked for rA_k'(r) and A_k(r) without verifying that these are C^1, nondecreasing and tend to ∞ as r → R^𝒮, which can fail (e.g. bounded A_k in the hyperbolic case).
